# Education in New Zealand – Overview
Education in New Zealand is free and compulsory between ages 6 and 16, with most children beginning primary school at age 5 and the majority continuing to secondary school until at least age 17. The system is divided into 13 year levels, encompassing eight years of primary education (including two years typically known as “intermediate”) and five years of secondary education. The school year runs from late January to mid-December, comprised of four terms. Schools are mainly classified as state (government-funded), state-integrated (retaining a special character, often religious, but funded similarly to state schools), and private (fee-based, with limited government support). State schools are governed by Boards of Trustees and follow the national curriculum, which covers eight key learning areas and transitions senior students to the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) or, in some cases, Cambridge International Examinations or International Baccalaureate.
Early childhood education is widespread and includes kindergarten, kōhanga reo (Māori immersion), playcentre, and day care, either centre-based or home-based, sometimes with specific educational philosophies. Funding for primary, secondary, and tertiary education is a mix of government support, voluntary parental donations, and for integrated/private schools, compulsory “attendance dues” or tuition fees. Māori language education is available as an immersion option (Kura Kaupapa Māori) or as a subject in mainstream schools, supported by legislation and targeted resourcing. The system has ongoing challenges, including disparities in achievement—particularly among Māori and Pacific Island students—and issues with bullying, educational standards in core subjects, and school funding adequacy.

# Curriculum, Tertiary Education, and Key Features
All state and integrated schools follow government curricula: The New Zealand Curriculum (NZC) for English-medium and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa for Māori-medium schools. The curriculum spans English/Māori language, mathematics and statistics, the arts, health/physical education, languages, science, social sciences, and technology. Most students in years 11–13 pursue NCEA qualifications, with options for CIE and IB. Tertiary education includes universities, polytechnics, and private institutions, with funding from government and student fees; financial support for students includes loans and means-tested allowances. The system strives to accommodate special needs through specialist schools and Ongoing Resource Scheme funding. Enrolment zones and schemes seek to balance school population and access but have led to socio-economic impacts. Throughout its history, New Zealand education has evolved from Māori wānanga and missionary schooling to today’s inclusive, multicultural system, with continual efforts to improve educational outcomes and equity.
